current_foundations.title: Can you trust what your agent remembers?
Why can a tool designed to block exfiltration still leak your data?
Does a high benchmark score predict production reliability?
Does compacting an agent's context put its safety rules at risk?
Can you trust an LLM-as-judge score?
How does speculative decoding speed up LLM inference?
Why does forcing structured output make my agent stop calling tools?

wiki_topics.title: Agent benchmarks: fixed tasks that exercise real tool use
wiki_topics.summary:
Pin down a fixed set of tasks with known good outcomes and run agents against
them repeatedly. Unlike model benchmarks, agent benchmarks have to exercise
*tool use and multi-step trajectories* — booking, querying, fixing, coordinating
— so they double as integration tests for the whole agent, not just the model.

wiki_topics.title: Agent token costs are unpredictable and easily run away
wiki_topics.summary:
A chatbot turn costs a predictable number of tokens; an agent can loop, re-read
its whole context every step, spawn sub-agents, and call a model to grade its
own work — so the bill is a function of *behavior*, not request count, and a
single misbehaving run or a topology choice can multiply spend without anyone
noticing until the invoice arrives. Cost is the run-time obstacle that the
build-time decisions (memory, multi-agent, eval) silently determine.

wiki_topics.title: Measuring whether an agent actually worked is hard
wiki_topics.summary:
A chatbot is graded on its final answer; an agent has to be graded on what it
*did* — the multi-step trajectory of tool calls, retries, and decisions that
led there. Outputs are non-deterministic, "correct-looking" answers can come
from broken paths, and a benchmark the agent has effectively memorized tells
you nothing about a new environment. Knowing whether an agent works in
production is itself an unsolved engineering problem.

wiki_topics.title: Agent loops multiply per-call latency into slow, expensive runs
wiki_topics.summary:
A chatbot waits on one model call; an agent waits on *many*, in sequence —
plan, call a tool, read the result, decide again — so the wall-clock a user
feels is the per-token decode latency multiplied by the loop length, and a
serving stack tuned for single-shot throughput can still leave an agent feeling
slow. Latency is the run-time twin of [cost](/topic/agent-cost): the same loop
that runs up the bill also runs out the clock.

wiki_topics.title: Agents forget across steps and sessions
wiki_topics.summary:
An agent's working memory is its context window, which is finite and resets
between runs. On long-horizon tasks it forgets earlier steps, repeats work, and
loses the user's intent — so "agent memory" (what to persist, where, and how to
recall it) becomes a first-class architecture problem rather than a prompt tweak.

wiki_topics.title: You can't see why an agent did what it did
wiki_topics.summary:
When an agent does the wrong thing, the run that produced it is a long,
non-deterministic chain of model calls, tool results, and intermediate decisions —
and most of that is invisible after the fact. Unlike a stack trace, an agent's
"why" is spread across a trajectory you didn't log in enough detail, can't replay
deterministically, and can't easily diff against a working run. Debugging an agent
is increasingly the job, not a footnote to it.

wiki_topics.title: Orchestration patterns: topologies, handoffs, and harnesses
wiki_topics.summary:
Orchestration is the control plane of a multi-agent system: how the work is
decomposed, which agent does what, how they hand off, and who — if anyone — is
in charge. The pattern you pick (central orchestrator vs. decentralized, a fixed
graph vs. one generated per task) sets the cost, latency, and reliability
ceiling of the whole system.

wiki_topics.title: Agents plan multi-step work badly — they loop, stall, or skip steps
wiki_topics.summary:
Give an agent a goal that takes ten steps and it will often take the wrong ones:
charge ahead on an ambiguous request instead of asking, decompose the task into a
plan that drifts, get stuck in a retry loop, or skip a step it needed. Planning —
turning a goal into the right ordered sequence of actions, and knowing when to stop
or ask — is a distinct failure mode from tool use or memory, and it's where
long-horizon agents most visibly fall down.

wiki_topics.title: Agents give fluent, confident-looking output even when it's wrong
wiki_topics.summary:
An agent can hallucinate a fact, skip a step, or misuse a tool and still
return a fluent, confident-looking answer — nothing about the output itself
signals that it's wrong. Deciding where to trust the model's own reasoning
versus routing to a deterministic tool, and getting an agent to actually
prove its work rather than just claim success, is a distinct engineering
problem from measuring that work after the fact (see
[agent evaluation](/topic/agent-evaluation)).

wiki_topics.title: Sandboxing, scoped credentials, and guardrails
wiki_topics.summary:
Assume the agent will be hijacked and limit the damage: run its code in a
sandbox, give it narrowly scoped and short-lived credentials, gate high-impact
actions behind approvals, and screen inputs/outputs with guardrails. None of
these stops injection on its own — together they shrink the blast radius of one
that gets through.

wiki_topics.title: Tracing and trace analysis for agent runs
wiki_topics.summary:
Capture every agent run as a structured trace — the prompts, tool calls, results,
retries, and sub-agent handoffs — in a common format, then analyze those traces to
find what broke and why. Tracing is the substrate that makes an agent debuggable,
evaluable, and operable instead of a black box that occasionally misbehaves.

wiki_topics.title: Context compaction: summarize, compress, and curate the working set
wiki_topics.summary:
Keep memory *inside* the context window but small: summarize old turns,
compress history, and deliberately curate what stays in-context each step
("context engineering"). The agent forgets less because the working set is
chosen, not just truncated.

wiki_topics.title: Cost controls: budgets, metering, and per-task attribution
wiki_topics.summary:
Make agent spend observable and bounded: meter token usage per task, user, and
tool; attribute it to the unit of work (a request, a PR); set budgets and hard
caps so a runaway loop trips a limit instead of the invoice; and cut fixed
overhead with caching. These are the operational guardrails that sit *around* an
agent, complementing the architectural levers (compaction, topology, cheap
judges) that reduce the underlying token count.

wiki_topics.title: An agent's answer is only as good as what it retrieved — and whether it can prove it
wiki_topics.summary:
A fluent agent answer isn't the same as a grounded one: the model will answer
past what it actually retrieved unless the retrieval was current, the right
slice, and cheap enough to fetch — and unless something checks that the
answer is actually backed by what came back. Grounding is the retrieval and
attribution problem underneath [agent memory](/topic/agent-memory); this
page tracks it as its own obstacle because retrieval quality and provenance
fail in ways a memory-tiering decision doesn't touch.

wiki_topics.title: LLM-as-judge: model-graded evaluation of traces and outputs
wiki_topics.summary:
Use a model to grade a model: give an LLM the agent's output (or its full
trace) plus a rubric, and have it return a structured verdict. It scales the
judgment human raters can't keep up with — every production trace, every CI
run — and is the practical backbone of agent evaluation when answers are
open-ended.

wiki_topics.title: Model Context Protocol: a standard interface for agent tools
wiki_topics.summary:
The Model Context Protocol (MCP) is a standard way to describe, discover, and
call tools so any MCP-speaking agent can use any MCP server. It collapses the
N×M problem of bespoke integrations into a common interface — the agent
equivalent of "speak HTTP" instead of writing a custom client per service.

wiki_topics.title: Agent behavior drifts as the model, SDK, and runtime churn under it
wiki_topics.summary:
An agent is built on a substrate you don't control and that moves faster than
your app: the underlying model gets upgraded or deprecated, the agent SDK and
orchestration framework ship multiple releases a week, and the serving runtime
changes its behavior under load. Every bump can silently change what the agent
does — or reintroduce a regression — between two deploys where *your* code never
changed. Drift is the run-time obstacle of maintenance: keeping a working agent
working as everything beneath it shifts.

wiki_topics.title: Coordinating multiple agents adds more failure than capability
wiki_topics.summary:
Splitting a job across several agents promises specialization and parallelism,
but every handoff is a lossy interface and each added agent multiplies the ways
the system can stall, loop, or disagree. Coordination overhead routinely eats
the gains — the hard part isn't building the agents, it's getting them to work
together without costing more than one good agent would.

wiki_topics.title: Untrusted input and tools can hijack an agent
wiki_topics.summary:
An agent treats whatever it reads — a web page, a tool result, a file, another
agent's message — as instructions it might follow. Prompt injection turns that
into an attack: hidden text redirects the agent to exfiltrate data, misuse its
tools, or escalate privileges. Because the agent has real credentials and can
act, a successful injection is not a bad answer — it's an unauthorized action.

wiki_topics.title: Proving agent ROI and measuring cost efficiency is hard
wiki_topics.summary: Calculating the true return on investment (ROI) for agent systems is blocked by the difficulty of measuring time-savings, tracking per-task token usage, and accounting for hidden costs like token inflation in low-bit quantized models. Platform engineers must transition from generic productivity claims to precise, instrumented cost-per-task accounting and evidence-based time-savings measurement.

wiki_topics.title: Speculative decoding: draft cheaply, verify in parallel
wiki_topics.summary:
Generate several candidate tokens cheaply with a small *draft* model (or a
lightweight head), then let the full model verify them in a single parallel
forward pass — accepted tokens come "for free," so latency drops without
changing the output distribution. It attacks the one term raw engine tuning
can't: the strictly sequential, one-token-at-a-time decode that dominates an
agent's wall-clock.

wiki_topics.title: Agents reach the outside world through fragile, ad-hoc integrations
wiki_topics.summary:
An agent is only as useful as the tools it can call, but every integration has
historically been bespoke: hand-written wrappers around REST APIs, brittle
schemas the model misuses, and no shared way to discover or authorize tools.
Connecting an agent to real systems — infra, browsers, SaaS — is where a lot of
the engineering actually goes, and it breaks in production in ways the model
never sees.

wiki_topics.title: External knowledge base: vector and graph retrieval
wiki_topics.summary:
Push long-term memory *out* of the context window into an external store —
embeddings in a vector index, and/or a knowledge graph of entities and
relations — and retrieve only the relevant slice at each step. This is how an
agent "remembers" more than fits in a prompt.

wiki_topics.title: Version pinning, compatibility ranges, and staged upgrades
wiki_topics.summary:
Treat the model, agent SDK, framework, and serving runtime as version-controlled
dependencies, not a rolling stream: pin exact versions, declare the compatibility
range you actually support, heed deprecation warnings, and promote upgrades
through a staged, tested path instead of tracking latest. It doesn't stop the
substrate from changing — it stops the change from reaching production
unnoticed.

latest_playbook_cards.title: Gate agent releases on three-tier eval scores, not vibes
latest_playbook_cards.problem: Motorway's dealer-search agent shipped with no way to catch tool-selection errors or multi-turn context drift before dealers saw them.
latest_playbook_cards.apply: Score every candidate release on three thresholds — tool usage >95%, reasoning >85%, output quality >90% — using strands-agents-evals pre-deploy and Bedrock AgentCore Evaluations in production, and block deployment in a five-stage pipeline when any threshold misses. For non-deterministic runs, track pass^k (success across k consecutive trials) instead of a single pass/fail.

latest_playbook_cards.title: Treat agent context as a lifecycle to manage, not a log to truncate
latest_playbook_cards.problem: Most production agent failures trace back to unmanaged context — bloated histories and tool definitions — not weak reasoning, and naive summarization trades accuracy for cost.
latest_playbook_cards.apply: Split context management into five explicit stages: architecting the context structure, ingesting new information, scoping it to what's organizationally relevant, anticipating what will be needed next, and compacting/consolidating while preserving provenance of every kept fact.

latest_playbook_cards.title: Offload multi-step logical reasoning to a Prolog MCP server, not the prompt
latest_playbook_cards.problem: LLMs hallucinate systematically on multi-step logical reasoning once a compliance or safety rule base gets large, and semantic RAG can't enforce hard rules.
latest_playbook_cards.apply: Expose a Prolog-backed MCP server (Euclid-MCP) that accepts a human-readable intermediate representation the LLM can generate directly, then run a translate-run-inspect-repair loop so the agent inspects proof traces and repairs its query instead of guessing at an answer.

latest_playbook_cards.title: Cut permission prompts by sandboxing the OS, not by asking more often
latest_playbook_cards.problem: Per-action approval prompts stopped protecting anything once users were approving about 93% of them on reflex.
latest_playbook_cards.apply: Replace prompt-based approval with OS-level sandboxes — Seatbelt on macOS, bubblewrap on Linux — that let the agent write inside its workspace but deny network access by default, and route any needed credentials through a proxy that only accepts a session-scoped token instead of raw secrets.

latest_playbook_cards.title: Codify security review into CLAUDE.md and skills before code generation, not after
latest_playbook_cards.problem: Manual security review can't scale once AI is authoring the majority of merged code — bugs need catching before they're generated, not after a human skims a diff.
latest_playbook_cards.apply: Encode your org's security guidelines directly in CLAUDE.md and skills so generated code follows them from the first draft, run /security-review to flag attacker-controllable input during development, and stack multiple narrow-scope review agents (each with RAG context, none with full-repo authority) ahead of a human reviewer who samples risk-weighted approvals.

latest_playbook_cards.title: Normalize retrieved-fact salience before your multi-hop RAG agent reasons over it
latest_playbook_cards.problem: A multi-hop RAG agent can be misled without a single false fact or injected instruction, just by reordering, emphasizing, or reframing truthful retrieved passages.
latest_playbook_cards.apply: Add Salience Normalization as an input-side defense: flatten framing, emphasis, and positional cues on retrieved passages before they reach the reasoning step, so attribute binding across hops can't be redirected by presentation alone.

latest_playbook_cards.title: Let the coding agent's own representations decide what context to prune
latest_playbook_cards.problem: Context-pruning for coding agents usually means running a separate classifier over tool output — another model to host, tune, and keep in sync.
latest_playbook_cards.apply: Attach a small head directly to the coding agent's own internal representations to emit a keep-or-prune label per line, using a length-aware embedding keyed to each tool output's line count, instead of standing up a separate pruning classifier.

latest_playbook_cards.title: Have the agent write specs, and a deterministic kernel write the code
latest_playbook_cards.problem: Agent-generated application code is hard to trust in production because there's no single artifact that's both the proof of correctness and the thing that actually runs.
latest_playbook_cards.apply: Have the agent emit a formal specification — behavior as a state machine, data as machine-readable entity definitions, authorization as default-deny policy — and let a deterministic kernel verify it via symbolic reasoning, exhaustive state exploration, fault-injected simulation, and property testing before it becomes the running system.
